name: Priya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play second violin for a community dance band, record slow practice lines for its beginners and teach two first-year pupils. I came to paid music after other work and finished secondary school; I am still learning from our lead fiddler when a fast set changes key. I like watching a nervous dancer find the beat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a booking hard to manage?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and my children are grown, but my partner’s bakery shifts and my small music fees still pay the rent. We have less than a month of expenses saved and few similar bands nearby. Retirement is in sight, yet I cannot put a date on stopping paid work from this account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a quicker booking message is fine if the player fee is still written beside the date. People do not dance to a tidy invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We are short of savings already, and my partner’s bakery hours change. A cancelled dance night would leave us choosing which bill to delay even if AI mostly stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid Friday dance sets, two pupils and simple practice recordings this season. I use AI now and then to sort dates, but I check the lead fiddler’s paper list; if a hall cancels, I would stop renting the practice booth that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about next month’s rent. A small technology change does not fix a thin account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the last cancelled dance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall flooded in spring and we lost a Friday fee. I would ask for a written half-fee cancellation term before the next hall season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown daughter cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own bills. I might ask for a lift to a paid rehearsal, but I would not count her wages as our savings.

say: I would welcome **quicker booking messages** if player fees stay beside dates.
I would say people do not dance to a **tidy invoice**.
think: Our **thin reserve** and variable bakery shifts make a cancelled night serious.
My **grown children** have bills of their own.
do: Keep **paid Friday sets**, two pupils and practice recordings this season.
Cancel **booth rental** if a dance night disappears; request a written half-fee term next season.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite a mild AI outcome.
S0.quote: People do not dance to a tidy invoice.
fieldNote: Her **junior playing** and low pay already leave less than one month saved.
Occasional **AI date sorting** is checked against the lead player’s paper list.

steps.text: Keep paid Friday dance sets, two pupils and simple recordings this season
Stop practice-booth rental if hall cancels a paid dance night
Request written half-fee cancellation term before next hall season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that generated practice lines could cost me the small recording orders. I would ask the leader for paid dance dates in writing before keeping Fridays clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those slow violin lines are about a third of my own music pay. The band still needs people on stage, but if recordings go I cannot replace them from a reserve shorter than one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the band leader for three months of paid dates and a paid demonstration of the centre’s new part-checking tool from our more experienced fiddler. In the first year I would test it on a simple violin part I own without pupil names, play every suggested note myself and stop if the range is wrong or the file leaves the centre; I would keep my two pupils while recording orders are checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely third of my pay disappearing. A new tool may help me avoid a wrong note, but it cannot turn an unpaid dance into a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the tool subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the paid demonstration must use the centre’s licence. I would stay with paper if I had to pay for a trial myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you send a pupil recording to the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No child’s playing goes into this test. My own plain part is enough for the lead fiddler to show me what it does.

say: I would warn generated practice lines threaten **recording orders**.
I would ask for **written paid dance dates** before holding Fridays.
think: My **practice recordings** provide about a third of my own pay.
A **sub-month reserve** cannot carry a long drop in those orders.
do: Request **three paid months** from the band leader next month.
Test **part checker** after paid mentor demo on owned nameless part; play changes and stop on range/privacy failure.
Keep **two pupils** while checking whether recording orders continue.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely lost recording pay and little savings.
S1.quote: A new tool may help me avoid a wrong note, but it cannot turn an unpaid dance into a wage.
fieldNote: Her **new tool trial** needs paid mentor instruction, centre licence, owned nameless part, manual playing and privacy stop.
She keeps **current pupils** while seeking written paid dates, not a guessed replacement job.

steps.text: Test centre-licensed checker after paid mentor demo on own nameless part; play changes, stop errors/leakage
Keep two beginner pupils while requesting three months of paid dance dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could make our beginner practice lines cheaply. Robots that can play a violin follow around 2031, three years later, so the recording cheque can go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect those small recording orders to end in 2028 and some halls may use generated backing. I cannot wait for a robot before asking where the rent money will come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would count practice-line invoices and ask for a signed paid dance calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid band nights fall too, I would seek a posted music-centre receptionist job only if my secondary education and customer experience meet its requirements, the written net wage after travel beats lost music fees and the hours fit our transport; I would keep band and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about expected lost recording pay and possible dance nights with almost no reserve. I have a plan to search, but a late offer will not pay next month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 60 when AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot promise that. We have not saved enough to stop working because of a date on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the centre just mentions a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing and teaching. I need a posted role, written hours and a real offer before I give notice.

say: I would warn **2028 thinking AGI** can make beginner practice lines cheaply.
I would distinguish lost **recording cheques** from violin robots around 2031.
think: I expect **recording orders** to end in 2028.
Paid **hall nights** may also shrink before any robot plays.
do: Count **practice invoices** and request signed paid dates this week.
Seek **posted centre work** after 2028 band cuts if schooling/customer experience qualify; written net after travel beats losses and transport hours fit.
Keep **band and pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected recording loss and an almost empty reserve.
S2.quote: I cannot wait for a robot before asking where the rent money will come from.
fieldNote: The likely **2028 recording loss** precedes 2031 playing robots.
The **centre move** needs actual band cuts, posted eligibility, written net replacement pay, transport fit and offer.

steps.text: Seek schooling/customer-experience-qualified posted centre job after band cuts; written replacement net after travel, transport hours fit
Keep paid band dates and pupils until suitable written centre offer is signed
Count practice invoices and request signed paid dance calendar now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to find another paid evening, not time to play free. Violin-playing robots follow around 2034, after the practice-line market changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recordings may end by 2031 and I will be 63. I could teach a few more beginners if families pay, but I cannot hire a room on the hope of names on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would secure written hire terms for an available room from a separate community hall before taking fees and offer a four-week beginner fiddle circle only if five adults prepay enough to cover hall hire, safe inspected loan violins and my teaching and preparation hours. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only while five still prepay those costs, written room terms hold and instruments are safe; I would keep my two current pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the group pays its way. Five years until AGI lets me test a paid fiddle circle without taking rent money for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan violin is damaged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall must check its loan violins and bows before anyone uses them. If it cannot, adults bring sound instruments while preserving five paid places, or I cancel and refund the whole circle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only three adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three fees will not cover the room and my preparation. I would refund them and keep the two pupils who already pay.

say: I would use **five years** to find another paid evening rather than play free.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AGI** from violin robots around 2034.
think: The **recordings** may end by 2031 before 2034 robots.
Five **prepaid adults** could fund room and teaching preparation.
do: Start **beginner circle** with written room terms and five prepayments covering hall, own teaching/preparation and safe inspected loans or sound own violins.
Repeat **after 2031** only on that five-place paid floor with written room and safe instruments; otherwise cancel/refund everyone.
Keep **two existing pupils** and refund three deposits if too few pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** until a separate group covers my own work.
S3.quote: Five years until AGI lets me test a paid fiddle circle without taking rent money for a deposit.
fieldNote: The **independent class** requires five prepayments covering hall and her own preparation, with no rent-money deposit.
Loan violins need **inspection** or adults bring sound instruments; three paid places trigger a refund.

steps.text: Start with written room terms, five prepayments covering hall/teaching/preparation, inspected loans or sound own violins
Renew after 2031 on same safe five-place floor and written room; cancel/refund all otherwise
Refund three deposits if too few pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to keep earning and plan carefully. Robots that can play a violin come around 2039, but a calendar does not say when I can afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need band and pupil pay. A decade to prepare matters, but our savings are under a month and I cannot invent retirement income that is not there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save ten percent of each extra paid dance fee after rent, food and travel until we have one month of expenses saved. In the first year after 2036 I would keep the paid pupils and band nights that remain and seek a posted music-centre desk job only if the dance fees fall, I meet the actual requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the hours fit our transport; I would leave current work only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious about the next rent payment even with ten years to plan. I would like to slow down, but I cannot name a retirement date from this account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra dance fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing from that source until a paying booking arrives. I would not cut food to make the savings line look tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a desk title for less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A written wage has to cover the lost band money after travel, not just sound more settled.

say: I would tell my children to **plan paid work** before slowing down.
I would keep **2036 thinking AGI** separate from 2039 violin robots.
think: At **68**, I may still need band and pupil fees.
Our **thin savings** do not support an assumed retirement date.
do: Save ten percent of **extra paid dance fees** after essentials toward one month of expenses.
Keep **paid band and pupils** after 2036 while bookings continue.
Seek **posted desk work** after 2036 dance cuts only if qualified, written net after travel replaces fees and transport fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current rent and later recording losses.
S4.quote: I cannot invent retirement income that is not there.
fieldNote: Her **one-month savings goal** uses only extra paid dance fees after essentials.
She would **keep earning at 68** unless a real paid desk offer replaces lost work.

steps.text: Save 10% of extra paid dance fees after rent, food and travel toward one month
Keep paid band nights and beginner pupils after 2036 while booked
Seek qualifying posted desk job after dance cuts; written replacement net after travel, transport hours fit
Keep current paid music until suitable signed desk offer arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-line orders could vanish before another paid job appears. Signed dance dates, a real centre opening that accepts my experience and written net pay above lost fees would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a beginner musician pays a bill between gigs at 58. I still practise scales before breakfast, but a scale does not pay the rent.

headlineQuote: I still practise scales before breakfast, but a scale does not pay the rent.
portrait: At **58**, Priya is a junior second violinist with secondary schooling, a partner, grown children and less than one month saved.
Her **lower music pay** comes from dance sets, two beginner pupils and simple practice lines in an area with few similar jobs.
She uses **AI occasionally** for dates and tests a new checker only after paid mentor instruction on owned nameless music.
She cannot assume **retirement income** will replace work at 60 or 68; every switch needs posted pay and transport fit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end practice-line orders before a real paid replacement job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed dance dates** and a posted eligible centre job with written net replacement pay would help Priya.
